title: Numbers that persuade
essentialQuestion: How can a chart or a number be true and still mislead you?
learningGoal: Explain how a chart's scale, a small survey and missing information can mislead, and use the real numbers to judge a claim.

sections.heading: A chart can stretch a small difference
sections.text: Charts help people understand numbers quickly and easily, so posters and news reports use them a lot. But a chart can also mislead you, even when every number on it is correct. At the Riverbend Sunday market, Stall A sells 52 bananas a day on average, and Stall B sells 50. On Stall A's poster, Stall A's bar looks three times as tall as Stall B's. How is that possible? The scale on the side of the chart begins at 49, not at zero. So Stall A's bar shows only the 3 bananas above 49, and Stall B's shows only 1. In a bar chart, people compare the heights of the bars, so the scale should start at zero.
sections.simpler: Charts help us see numbers fast. But a chart can mislead you. Even its numbers can all be right. Stall A sells 52 bananas a day. Stall B sells 50. On Stall A's poster, its bar looks three times as tall. Why? The scale starts at 49, not at zero. So the bars show only a small part. Stall A's bar shows 3. Stall B's bar shows 1. In a bar chart, the scale should start at zero.

sections.heading: Ask who was asked, and how many
sections.text: Stall A's poster also says, “8 out of 10 shoppers prefer our bananas”. That sounds impressive, as if 80 per cent of all shoppers agree. But the small print says the stall asked only 10 people, and all of them were its own regular shoppers. A survey of a few people who already like one stall can't tell you what most shoppers think. When you see a number from a survey, ask two questions. Who was asked? How many people were asked? A bigger group, chosen fairly, usually gives a more trustworthy answer than a small group chosen by the seller.
sections.simpler: The poster also says, “8 out of 10 shoppers like our bananas best”. That sounds like a lot. But Stall A asked only 10 people. All 10 already shop at Stall A. So the survey does not show what most shoppers think. Ask two questions about a survey. Who was asked? How many were asked? A big group, chosen fairly, is better.

sections.heading: Look for what is missing
sections.text: Charts and numbers can also mislead by leaving things out. A poster might show only the one day when Stall B ran out of bananas early, and hide all the other days. Choosing only the numbers that help your side is called cherry-picking. So whenever a chart or a number tries to persuade you, slow down and check four things. Read the labels, look at the actual numbers, check where the scale starts, and ask what might be missing. Then do the maths yourself, because a quick calculation often tells the real story. For Stall A, 52 take away 50 is just 2 bananas a day, not three times as many.
sections.simpler: Numbers can also mislead by leaving things out. A poster could show only one day. Maybe Stall B ran out of bananas that day. Picking only the numbers that help you is called cherry-picking. So check four things. Read the labels. Look at the numbers. Check where the scale starts. Ask what is missing. Then do the maths. 52 take away 50 is 2. That is a small difference.

glossary.definition: A picture that shows numbers, for example with bars or lines.
glossary.example: Stall A's poster has a bar chart of bananas sold.

glossary.definition: The numbers along the side of a chart.
glossary.example: The scale on Stall A's chart starts at 49.

glossary.definition: To make someone believe something that is not true.
glossary.example: The tall bar can mislead shoppers.

glossary.definition: Asking a group of people the same questions to learn what they think.
glossary.example: Stall A's survey asked only 10 people.

glossary.definition: Choosing only the facts that help your side and hiding the rest.
glossary.example: Showing only the day Stall B ran out of bananas is cherry-picking.

write.example: Stall A's poster says it sells three times more bananas than Stall B. The chart looks that way because the scale starts at 49, not at zero. The real numbers are 52 bananas a day for Stall A and 50 for Stall B, so the difference is only 2. The survey only asked 10 of Stall A's own shoppers. An honest poster would start the scale at zero and say how many people were asked, and who.

watch.title: How to spot a misleading graph - Lea Gaslowitz
watch.why: This animated lesson uses real examples to show how a graph can mislead.
watch.beforeQuestion: Can a chart mislead you if every number on it is true?
watch.afterQuestion: What four things does the video say to look at in a graph?
watch.summary: This animated lesson explains how graphs can mislead. Many people trust a graph because it shows numbers, not opinions. But graphs can still trick us. The most common trick is changing the scale. One advert used a scale that went only from 95 to 100 per cent. A tiny difference between two kinds of truck looked huge. This trick is worst in bar graphs, because we expect the size of the bars to match the numbers. A graph can also choose a time range, or a few points, that hide what really happened. This is called cherry-picking. A graph can also leave out facts that matter, like a growing population. At the end, the video says to look at the labels, the numbers, the scale and the context before you trust a graph.
keyPoints: A scale that does not start at zero can make a tiny difference look huge.
Cherry-picking a time range or a few points can hide what really happened.
Look at the labels, the numbers, the scale and the context.
watch.contentNote: TED-Ed animation, 3 minutes 49 seconds, in fast English. Its examples name real companies (a 1992 truck advert from Chevy, compared with Toyota), US unemployment figures, the Super Bowl and ocean temperatures, and it mentions advertising and politicians. educatorNotes: Maths as reasoning, not drills: 52 take away 50 is 2. On the poster the bars show only the part above 49 (3 and 1), so one looks three times as tall. Paper version of the activity: draw both charts on squared paper, one starting at 49 and one at zero.

The “start at zero” rule is for bar charts. Line charts that show change over time don't always need to start at zero (Calling Bullshit). A bigger survey is better only when the people are chosen fairly (Full Fact).
Some learners have had little maths at school. Nothing here is a test: let partners work out the difference together, and use the words “take away”.
